La lectura es un cuento.
Mi abuelo vendía elotes en la esquina de la plaza desde antes de que yo naciera. Cada tarde, a las cinco, empujaba su carrito de lámina hasta el mismo lugar, bajo el jacarandá,
y encendía el anafre con la paciencia de un relojero. Yo lo acompañaba los sábados, y mi tarea era aparentemente sencilla: contar las monedas y no perder de vista las
mazorcas.
Lo que más me asombraba era su manera de atender. Conocía a todos por su nombre y recordaba lo que cada cliente prefería: con chile, sin mayonesa, con mucho limón. «Un
elote no se vende —decía—; se entrega, como se entrega un recado importante.»
Cuando el abuelo murió, el carrito se quedó varias semanas arrumbado en el patio, cubierto de polvo. Un sábado, sin pensarlo demasiado, lo limpié, lo llené de mazorcas y lo
llevé hasta el jacarandá. La primera clienta, una señora de abrigo gris, me miró con ternura. «Con mucho limón, ¿verdad?», le pregunté. Ella sonrió, y por un instante sentí que el
abuelo estaba parado a mi lado.

questions.passage:
In this passage from a short story, a young man named Tomás helps his grandmother close her bakery for the last time.
(1) The bell above the door gave its usual tired jingle as Tomás turned the sign to CERRADO.
(2) Behind the counter, his grandmother was wiping down a surface that was already spotless,
moving her cloth in the slow circles she had used for forty years. (3) “You will wear a hole in
the wood,” he said gently, but she did not answer, and he understood that the cleaning was not
really about the counter.
(4) The shop smelled the way it always had, of cinnamon and scorched sugar, and the smell
seemed to Tomás almost unfair, as though the building had not been told. (5) On the shelves
behind her, the glass jars stood empty, their lids stacked in a neat tower beside the register. (6)
For weeks his grandmother had insisted that she was tired of the early mornings and the
burned fingertips, that her knees would thank her. (7) Yet she had never once suggested that
the oven be sold; it sat in the corner, cold and enormous, like a patient animal waiting to be
called.
(8) “Abuela,” he said, “we can still come back on Sunday.” (9) She folded the cloth into a square,
then into a smaller square, and set it on the counter with great care. (10) “Sunday it will be
somebody else’s,” she said. (11) Then she smiled, not at him but at the oven, and her face
loosened in a way he had not seen in months. (12) “But this morning,” she added, “it was mine,
and the bread was good.”
(13) Tomás did not trust his voice, so he reached for the light switch instead. (14) For a
moment the shop hung in the dim gold of late afternoon, every surface glowing as if it, too,
were reluctant to leave. (15) Then his grandmother took his arm, and together they stepped out
into the street, where she did not look back, and where he looked back for both of them.

meet neighbors they otherwise would not, and several city studies report fewer
